questions.prompt: The cabin has a volume of 24 × 2.4 = 57.6 m³ and 0.5 air changes per hour. What is the ventilation loss H = 0.33 n V, in W/K to 1 decimal place?
questions.onCorrect: This is the largest single term in the cabin’s budget, so sealing gaps pays back more than adding to the walls.

misconceptions.feedback: 19 uses 1 air change an hour. The rate here is 0.5.

questions.prompt: A 9 m wall stands at latitude 50 degrees north, where the noon sun altitude on 21 December is 16.56 degrees. How long is the wall’s noon shadow, in metres to the nearest metre?
hints: Rearrange to shadow = height ÷ tan(altitude), with your calculator in degree mode.
questions.onCorrect: 9 ÷ tan 16.56° = 9 ÷ 0.2974 = 30.3, so the shadow is about 30 m, more than three times the height of the wall.

misconceptions.feedback: About 2.7 m comes from multiplying 9 by tan 16.56°. The tangent is height over shadow, so the shadow is the height divided by it.
About 10.7 m uses the equinox altitude of 40 degrees. On 21 December the declination lowers it to 16.56 degrees.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Shadow = 9 ÷ tan 16.56° = 9 ÷ 0.2974 = 30.3, which is 30 m to the nearest metre.

questions.prompt: The room air has a dew point of 13.2 °C, and the inside surface of an insulated wall is at 19.55 °C. What happens on that surface?
hints: Compare the surface temperature with the dew point. Which one is lower?
questions.onCorrect: Water forms only where a surface is colder than the dew point, and this wall is more than six degrees warmer than it.

misconceptions.feedback: Condensation needs a surface colder than the dew point. At 19.55 °C this wall is well above 13.2 °C, so the air beside it never reaches saturation.
Freezing needs a temperature below 0 °C, and this surface is at 19.55 °C.
The two temperatures are enough: a surface above the dew point stays dry.

questions.prompt: A concrete lintel bridges the insulation, and its inside surface is at 16.88 °C while the plain wall beside it is at 19.55 °C. On a humid day the room air’s dew point rises to 17.5 °C. What happens?
hints: Compare each surface with the new dew point.
Only a surface colder than 17.5 °C collects water.
questions.onCorrect: The damp appears along the line of the bridge first, which is why a cold lintel shows as a dark stripe above a window long before the rest of the wall is affected.

misconceptions.feedback: The plain wall, at 19.55 °C, is warmer than the 17.5 °C dew point, so it stays dry. The lintel is the colder of the two surfaces.
Water forms on any surface colder than the dew point, not only below freezing. The lintel, at 16.88 °C, is below 17.5 °C.
The room air is at 20 °C, but what matters is each surface’s own temperature. The lintel, at 16.88 °C, is below the dew point.

acceptedIdeas: Water forms on the lintel while the plain wall stays dry
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Water forms on the lintel while the plain wall stays dry

choices.label: Water forms on the plain wall but not on the lintel
Both stay dry, since both surfaces are well above 0 °C
Both stay dry, since the room air is at 20 °C
Water forms on the lintel while the plain wall stays dry

questions.prompt: Why is the heat a person gives off found by multiplying the met value by the area of their skin?
hints: Look at the unit of one met.
questions.onCorrect: Because a met is a rate per square metre, a larger person doing the same work gives off proportionally more heat.

misconceptions.feedback: The skin area does not change the units from degrees to watts. A met is already in watts, per square metre of skin.
The calculation does not depend on how warm the person feels. It counts the heat produced, which is a rate per square metre of skin.

acceptedIdeas: A met is a rate of heat per square metre of skin, so the total grows with the skin area
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A met is a rate of heat per square metre of skin, so the total grows with the skin area

choices.label: Multiplying by the skin area turns degrees into watts
A met is a rate of heat per square metre of skin, so the total grows with the skin area
A person with more skin feels warmer

questions.prompt: A 1:100 drawing made on A1 is printed at 50 percent on A3. The print’s scale is 1:n. What is n?
hints: Halving every paper length doubles the ratio of real length to paper length.
questions.onCorrect: The print is at 1:200, the scale of a site plan, so a room that was 42 mm wide on the original is only 21 mm wide on it.

misconceptions.feedback: 50 halves the ratio, which would make the print larger than the original. Halving the paper lengths doubles the ratio instead.
100 is the scale of the original. Once every paper length is halved, a metre of building takes half as much paper, so the ratio doubles.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At 50 percent each paper length is halved, so the ratio doubles from 1:100 to 1:200.

flashcards.front: Latitude 52. What is the noon sun altitude at the December solstice, in degrees to one decimal place?
The sun rises due east on which two dates?
flashcards.back: At the equinoxes the declination is zero, so the sun rises due east and sets due west.

flashcards.front: Why does a fixed overhang over a south window help in both seasons?
flashcards.back: In June the sun is high, so the overhang shades the glass; in December the sun is low, so its shadow barely reaches the glass.

flashcards.front: Net area 85 m² at 85 percent efficiency. Gross area in m²?
What is the term for the list of spaces a building must provide, with their areas and relationships?
flashcards.back: The programme says what the building must contain before its form is chosen.

flashcards.front: Why is net area never the same as the footprint?
flashcards.back: Walls, corridors, stairs and services need floor area that is not inside any room, so gross is larger than net.

flashcards.front: A room is 4.2 m wide. Its width on paper at 1:50 in millimetres?
Which view is a horizontal cut about 1.2 m above the floor?
flashcards.back: A floor plan cuts through walls, windows and doors so the rooms can be read.

flashcards.front: What does 1:50 mean, and which way do you convert?
flashcards.back: 1 unit on paper stands for 50 in the building: multiply paper by 50 for real, divide real by 50 for paper.

flashcards.front: Riser 168.75 mm. What going does 2R + G = 630 give, in millimetres?
What is the name of the horizontal depth of one step?
flashcards.back: The going is the horizontal distance from one riser to the next.

flashcards.front: Why is a steep stair a safety issue and not only a comfort one?
flashcards.back: A steep stair makes missteps and falls more likely, which is why codes limit the pitch as well as recommending a comfortable rule.

flashcards.front: Floor design load 2.925 kN/m² on joists at 0.4 m. Line load in kN/m?
What is the name for the continuous route that carries loads from the roof and floors to the ground?
flashcards.back: The load path must be unbroken, so every load has a member under it all the way to the ground.

flashcards.front: Why is the area load multiplied by the joist spacing?
flashcards.back: Each joist carries a strip of floor as wide as the spacing, so kN per square metre times metres gives kN per metre.

flashcards.front: Indoors 150 lux, outdoors 10 000 lux. Daylight factor in percent?
In the depth rule L/W + L/Hw ≤ 2/(1 − R), what does R stand for?
flashcards.back: R is the average reflectance of the room’s surfaces, a number between 0 and 1.

flashcards.front: Why is window area alone a poor measure of how well lit a room is?
flashcards.back: Where the window sits matters too: a higher window lights deeper, and the room’s depth and reflectances change how much reaches the back.

flashcards.front: Brick 102 mm, conductivity 0.77. Thermal resistance in m²K/W to 3 decimal places?
What do you do to the layer resistances and surface resistances to find the U-value?
flashcards.back: Add all the resistances, then take the reciprocal: U = 1 ÷ (Rsi + sum of R + Rse).

flashcards.front: Why do insulation materials have low conductivity rather than great thickness being the key?
flashcards.back: Resistance is thickness divided by conductivity, so a layer with a conductivity 35 times lower resists 35 times more at the same thickness.

flashcards.front: V = 150 m³ at 0.5 air changes per hour. H = 0.33 n V in W/K?
What is the name for the temperature at which air of a given moisture content becomes saturated?
flashcards.back: Below this temperature water condenses out of the air onto surfaces.

flashcards.front: Why does an airtight house need deliberate ventilation?
flashcards.back: Without gaps, moisture and pollutants from people and cooking stay in, so fresh air must be supplied on purpose, ideally with heat recovery.

flashcards.front: 1 met is 58.2 W/m² and a person has 1.8 m² of skin. Heat at 1 met in watts to the nearest watt?
What is the average of the air temperature and the mean radiant temperature (at low air speed) called?
flashcards.back: Operative temperature approximates what a person feels, combining air and radiant temperature.

flashcards.front: Name the three ways a body loses heat and which one a cold wall changes.
flashcards.back: Radiation, convection and evaporation; a cold wall increases radiation to it, so the room feels colder than the air temperature suggests.

flashcards.front: A 6 m span at 30 degrees. Ridge rise above the eaves in metres to 2 decimal places?
Which area of a roof is used to compute rainwater flow: plan area or sloped area?
flashcards.back: Rain falls vertically, so the plan area, the area seen from above, is what the rain lands on.

flashcards.front: Why must a damp-proof course stay above the ground, and not only stop rising damp?
flashcards.back: Rain splash and soil piled against the wall above the course carry water past it, so the course must clear the ground.

flashcards.front: A 12 m wall at 1:100. Length on paper in millimetres?
What are the thin lines with arrows that show lengths on a plan called?
flashcards.back: Dimension strings give lengths in tiers, so a builder can read each one without scaling the drawing.

flashcards.front: Why are drawings called instructions and not pictures?
flashcards.back: They tell the builder what to build and, with the contract, define what the client has paid for, so they must be complete and to scale.

flashcards.front: 6 m × 4 m at 85 percent efficiency. Net area in m² to 1 decimal place?
What is the name for reducing heat loss through the building envelope before adding heating systems?
flashcards.back: Fabric first means insulating and sealing the envelope so that any heating system can be smaller.

flashcards.front: Give one example of a decision in the cabin that affects another.
flashcards.back: The south glazing admits winter sun and daylight but adds heat loss and summer overheating, so its area is set by all three.
